value.overview: The White-necked Puffbird (Notharchus hyperrhynchus) is a large, broad-headed puffbird of tropical lowlands from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern and western South America. It is usually encountered alone or in pairs, sitting quietly on an exposed branch before making a short flight to seize prey. Its striking plumage combines a dark crown and back, a broad black breast band, white throat and neck, and a heavy dark bill.
value.classification: The species belongs to the puffbird family Bucconidae in the order Galbuliformes. It is closely related to other large Notharchus puffbirds.
value.identification: This compact, large-headed bird has a very heavy black bill, dark upperparts, a white forehead and throat, and a broad black band across the upper breast. The lower breast and belly are generally white, while the wings and back can show fine pale markings. It often perches upright and motionless on a bare horizontal branch, sometimes high in the canopy. Its long, steady, bubbling or rolling trill is distinctive when heard.
value.rangeHabitat: The White-necked Puffbird ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to Colombia, Ecuador, and parts of the Amazon Basin. In Costa Rica it is a resident, widely distributed but generally uncommon species of the lowlands on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, especially below about 600 meters. It uses humid evergreen and semi-evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings, secondary woodland, open areas with scattered trees, plantations, and sometimes mangrove margins. It may occur from ground level to the canopy.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered nonmigratory and resident in Costa Rica. Individuals remain in the country year-round rather than arriving as seasonal migrants, although local movements may follow food availability or breeding conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited and varies across the range. Pairs excavate nest cavities, often in arboreal termite nests or rotten wood; cavities in earth banks or other substrates have also been reported. The nest is usually several meters above the ground when placed in a tree. Clutches are reported to contain about two white eggs, and both adults are believed to share incubation and care of the young. In tropical regions, breeding generally occurs during the wetter part of the year.
value.dietFeeding: The species is mainly an insect-eater, taking large beetles, grasshoppers, cicadas, ants, and other arthropods. It also captures small lizards and other small vertebrates, and occasional plant material may be taken. Its characteristic hunting method is to sit motionless on an exposed perch, make a short sally to seize prey, and return to a branch where the prey may be beaten before being swallowed. It sometimes investigates army-ant swarms.
value.behavior: White-necked Puffbirds are quiet, inconspicuous birds that are usually seen singly, in pairs, or in small family groups. They spend long periods sitting still and can be difficult to detect in dense forest. Their slow, deliberate movements contrast with rapid short flights to feeding sites. Pairs may defend territories and vocalize with prolonged, even-pitched trills, descending whistles, or softer calls. The species uses several forest layers but is often noticed on exposed branches in the canopy or at forest edges.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although it remains widespread and is not currently classified as threatened.
